notes.meaning: Zechariah sees a huge scroll flying through the air. A scroll was a long rolled-up sheet used for writing, like a book. It is spread open and moving fast, which shows that God's word of judgment goes out quickly. Because it is written down, its message is sure and cannot be taken back.

The scroll is about thirty feet long and fifteen feet wide. That is the same size as the porch of Solomon's temple and the holy room of the tabernacle (the tent where Israel worshiped). Some older teachers say this shows sinners will be measured by the standard of God's holy place. Its great size also hints at how many curses hang over those who break God's law.

The angel explains that the scroll is God's curse going out over the land. It is written on both sides, like the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments. One side is against thieves, who wrong their neighbor. The other is against perjurers, people who lie under oath, and so dishonor God. These two sins stand for breaking both halves of God's law, and the guilty will be cleared away.

The LORD himself sends the curse, so no one can stop it. It goes right into the home of the thief and the liar, where he feels safest, and no lock can keep it out. It settles there and eats up the house, even its wood and stones. Some older teachers link the theft to people robbing God by neglecting His temple while building their own houses.

The angel shows Zechariah a second sight: a measuring basket called an ephah, which held about a bushel of grain. The angel says it pictures the wickedness of the people in the land. Some older teachers say it shows sinners being gathered together like grains in a basket. Others say it shows that God keeps wickedness under His control, in a measure He can open or shut.

A heavy lead lid is lifted, and a woman is sitting inside the basket. The angel names her Wickedness, meaning sin itself. When she tries to rise, he shoves her back down and slams the heavy lid shut. This shows that sin is shut up like a prisoner and cannot escape God's judgment. Guilt presses on the sinner like a crushing weight.

Two women with wings like a stork's come and lift the basket into the sky. Storks have wide, strong wings, and the wind helps them fly fast. This shows God carrying out His plan quickly, using whatever helpers He chooses. Lifting the basket between heaven and earth means the judgment happens in open view.

The basket is taken to Shinar, the land of Babylon, where people once built the tower of Babel against God. A house is built there for Wickedness, so she will stay there for good, in the home that fits her. Many older teachers see comfort here: God removes sin far from His people so the land can be clean. Some, like Matthew Henry and Wesley, also saw a warning that God's people would be scattered for a long time if they kept sinning.
